This is Trending Not Peak. Quick note: this podcast uses AI-assisted writing and a synthetic voice. Before we dive in, all the links and details are at trending not peak dot com. Miss something? You can always catch up there.

14 stories. Tap one for its transcript, why we picked it, and source links:

  • 01 · Ask a model to edit another model's weights
  • 02 · Laya makes typed decisions in one pass
  • 03 · Forecast related time series together
  • 04 · Rustable puts database edits up for review
  • 05 · The first reasoning tokens change controllability
  • 06 · AMD tutorials launch into prepared GPU environments
  • 07 · A forge audit traces a path to upstream access
  • 08 · Embed Office-file editing in a browser
  • 09 · An MLX reference pack preserves released precision
  • 10 · Tor can hide page names from window titles
  • 11 · Validate the infrastructure beneath model serving
  • 12 · Practice Vim through small real edits
  • 13 · Study a raycasting game built in Python
  • 14 · A personal art museum gets a sculpture hall

Full transcript · All story details and sources

Ask a model to edit another model's weights

First up, weight-space programming asks a language model to change neural-network weights directly. MIT researchers report that GPT-6 Astra edited just zero point zero one six percent of a small Qwen model's weights, raising MATH-500 accuracy from seven point nine to forty-eight point one percent under the same sampling settings. That's an intriguing experiment for interpretability researchers: investigate a behavior, then test a targeted repair. Independent reproduction would make this much more interesting.

Source 1 Source 2

Laya makes typed decisions in one pass

From the editor's desk, Laya is worth knowing about if your pipeline needs a decision rather than a paragraph. Convai Innovations' Apache-licensed model answers typed questions in one forward pass: choose an option, assign a score, or answer yes or no. You can install it today for routing experiments. The base checkpoints perform near chance on typed decisions, though, so plan to fine-tune and calibrate confidence using your own examples.

Source 1 Source 2 Source 3

Forecast related time series together

Another editor's desk pick: Google's TimesFM-three forecasts several related time series together, including inputs known in advance, such as promotions. Analysts could use it to establish a demand or capacity baseline without training a separate model for every series. Released in August, it produces a forecast and uncertainty quantiles in one pass. Self-hosted version-three weights prohibit both commercial and production use; Google offers those uses through Cloud, including BigQuery.

Source 1 Source 2 Source 3 Source 4

Rustable puts database edits up for review

Over at the database desk, Rustable is a newly introduced native client supporting PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL, MariaDB and standalone Redis. It includes SSH tunnels, saved queries and row edits you review before saving. Database developers can explore the browser demo with disposable data before downloading the desktop app. Server connections require that app, and Redis Cluster and Sentinel aren't included. A useful first task is checking how clearly it presents a pending edit.

Source 1 Source 2

The first reasoning tokens change controllability

Turning to model oversight, a new paper finds that the first few reasoning tokens can strongly affect how well models follow instructions about their reasoning traces. Banning common openings and adding examples improved compliance by thirty-four to forty-one percentage points across tested models. Evaluation builders could use this to separate an awkward opening from a broader control limitation. Adding or restyling information improved more consistently than suppressing it, so those abilities deserve separate tests.

Source 1 Source 2

AMD tutorials launch into prepared GPU environments

For some hands-on GPU time, five AMD tutorials now open directly in Developer Cloud with prepared MI300 environments. Options include vision-model OCR, a PydanticAI agent using vLLM, and Triton kernel development. That gives developers exploring AMD hardware a shorter route from reading a notebook to running it. Cloud sign-in is required. Pick a familiar workload first, so you can spend the session comparing behavior rather than wondering whether your setup is broken.

Source 1 Source 2

A forge audit traces a path to upstream access

On the security side, Hacktron's new account traces a GNU Savannah compromise from an email-address shell injection to the ability to add a key with upstream Bash push access. The researchers say they reported the chain and helped the FSF fix twenty-six vulnerabilities. They describe access, not a planted Bash backdoor. Forge maintainers get a concrete audit exercise: follow user-controlled fields through command execution, account administration and repository permissions.

Source 1 Source 2

Thanks to Intelligrit, this episode's sponsor. Your support helps us make room for experiments worth opening up and understanding.

Embed Office-file editing in a browser

Back to building interfaces, office-engine has launched a browser toolkit for viewing and editing Word, Excel and PowerPoint files, then saving their original formats. Its React embed and progressive loading could help developers add document review to an existing application. The creator claims a three-hundred-thousand-row spreadsheet opens in about three hundred milliseconds; that's a launch measurement to reproduce. Start with a troublesome real file and check what survives a save and reopen.

Source 1 Source 2

An MLX reference pack preserves released precision

Meanwhile, on very large Macs, a community DeepSeek V4.1 Flash pack preserves the released weight precision in MLX layout. It's a reference for comparing smaller quantized packs, giving local-inference developers an artifact to investigate. The download is about four hundred seventy-seven gigabytes. A contributor reports running it on an M3 Ultra with five hundred twelve gigabytes; the pack authors couldn't load it on their own five-hundred-twelve-gigabyte machine. Reproducing that setup comes first.

Source 1 Source 2

Tor can hide page names from window titles

Over in browser privacy, Tor Browser sixteen adds an option to replace page-specific window titles with simply Tor Browser. That closes one way other desktop applications can learn which pages you're viewing. Privacy-tool developers can explore a small interface choice with a surprisingly useful effect. It's opt-in because accessibility and desktop integration effects haven't been fully evaluated. If you use a screen reader or a customized window switcher, that interaction is worth testing carefully.

Source 1 Source 2

Validate the infrastructure beneath model serving

Down in the cluster, NVIDIA's AI Cluster Runtime packages Dynamo's supporting infrastructure into recipes with pinned versions and validation checks. Platform engineers can use the new walkthrough to configure drivers, scheduling and networking before deploying model workloads. That's useful when a serving failure could come from several layers below your application. The concrete experiment is deploying a recipe into a test cluster, then checking whether its validation catches the configuration mistakes you actually encounter.

Source 1 Source 2

Practice Vim through small real edits

For a smaller learning loop, hjkl is a newly launched browser game for practicing Vim through actual editing tasks. Choose motions, text objects or repeats, then work through guided and independent exercises. Any valid edit reaching the target passes, so you're free to discover another route. It's free, requires no account, and needs a desktop browser with a physical keyboard. Pick one command you keep forgetting and give your fingers a useful five-minute assignment.

Source 1 Source 2

Study a raycasting game built in Python

Taking a retro turn, PyWolf3D is a newly shared Wolfenstein-style engine and game clone written from scratch in Python and Pygame. The creator built it for fun and learning, with map parsing, rendering and actor behavior in the public code. Aspiring engine developers could follow how those pieces become a playable scene, then change one mechanic. The repository includes instructions for the first episode's shareware version. There's your excuse to study raycasting between corridor patrols.

Source 1 Source 2

A personal art museum gets a sculpture hall

And finally, a developer built a virtual museum for his wife's artwork, then added a sculpture hall with a model reconstructed from photographs. Visitors can walk around, change the weather and adjust the time of day. Artists and web developers could borrow the idea for a personal exhibition that feels like a place. Mobile performance is still being tuned. The creator also recommends turning on rain if you like cats. That's a very specific museum forecast.

Source 1 Source 2

This is Trending Not Peak. Quick note: this podcast uses AI-assisted writing and a synthetic voice. Before we dive in, all the links and details are at trending not peak dot com. Miss something? You can always catch up there.

12 stories. Tap one for its transcript, why we picked it, and source links:

  • 01 · Corgi shares Rust builds across worktrees
  • 02 · DeepSeek shares an internal agent experiment
  • 03 · Phoria2 rebuilds a small web 3D toolkit
  • 04 · OpenMed adds a larger disease extractor
  • 05 · PostgreSQL's bug-finding bottleneck moves
  • 06 · Org's rewritten math previews stay responsive
  • 07 · Sakana starts its own pretraining program
  • 08 · GEFS gains OpenBSD filesystem creation tools
  • 09 · A Haskell processor learns to talk
  • 10 · Explore an eight-bit computer on virtual breadboards
  • 11 · A dangling string view haunts a permission check
  • 12 · Jointter hides words in a dot-and-line graph

Full transcript · All story details and sources

Corgi shares Rust builds across worktrees

First up, Corgi tackles something Rust developers with several worktrees know painfully well: compiling the same dependencies again. It shares a machine-wide build cache, caches successful tests, and restricts build scripts so stray environment changes don't wreck reuse. You can experiment locally while keeping Cargo in CI. Currently, it supports macOS and NixOS; other Linux distributions and Windows are in progress. A useful first test: switch branches and see how much work actually repeats.

Source 1 Source 2

DeepSeek shares an internal agent experiment

Next up, DeepSeek has published a research prototype that grew out of its team's everyday development work. The repository includes source, prompts, skills and examples, giving agent builders something concrete to inspect when exploring more autonomous workflows. Much of its engineering was itself done by coding agents. This isn't an official DeepSeek product, and the published version differs from the internal system. Pick one mechanism to study before borrowing the whole machine.

Source 1 Source 2

Phoria2 rebuilds a small web 3D toolkit

Turning to browser graphics, Phoria2 rebuilds a canvas library from twenty thirteen around WebGL two. It packages labels, picking, shadows and model loading without runtime dependencies, and only redraws views when something changes. That gives dashboard developers a compact option for interactive diagrams or product viewers. Its option validation also returns errors explaining the fix, which could help coding agents recover. Start with a labeled scene and see whether the API fits your project.

Source 1 Source 2

OpenMed adds a larger disease extractor

Back to local AI. We covered OpenMed's smaller disease extractor on October thirtieth; this release adds a 576-million-parameter GLiFormer checkpoint. It runs on a CPU and returns disease mentions with character offsets and confidence scores. OpenMed reports sixty-nine F1 on BC5CDR, which it says wasn't training data. Biomedical developers now have another checkpoint to compare for document indexing. The useful comparison includes missed mentions and processing time, plus whether surrounding text says the disease is actually present.

Source 1 Source 2

PostgreSQL's bug-finding bottleneck moves

Meanwhile, PostgreSQL contributor Robert Haas describes an unexpected consequence of AI-assisted bug hunting: finding problems faster than maintainers can review fixes. His new account connects that pressure with PostgreSQL nineteen's delayed release and late feature reversions. He reports over sixty percent more backpatched commits in the compared release-development periods. Open-source contributors could use this as a prompt to pair bug reports with careful reproductions and tested fixes. Finding the bug is increasingly the beginning of the work.

Source 1 Source 2

Org's rewritten math previews stay responsive

For people writing technical notes, Org mode's rewritten LaTeX previews bring asynchronous rendering and near-live visual feedback to Emacs. The implementation is available in Org's development branch, and a new explanation walks through its event loop, subprocesses and image overlays. Researchers can explore a smoother math-writing workflow; package authors get a substantial case study in responsive editor features. You can keep the editable text and see the equation take shape around it.

Source 1 Source 2 Source 3

We're halfway through today's finds. Thank you to Intelligrit, this episode's sponsor, for helping us keep these useful little discoveries coming.

Sakana starts its own pretraining program

Looking ahead, Sakana AI has announced that it's developing language models from pretraining onward, under the provisional Sawara name. Its first small model is planned for spring twenty twenty-seven, if development goes smoothly. Researchers interested in alternatives to simply scaling larger models can explore the newly published symposium report, including its world-model and autonomous-discovery directions. There's no new checkpoint to download here. The concrete thing to follow is how those research ideas become an inspectable small model.

Source 1 Source 2

GEFS gains OpenBSD filesystem creation tools

Down in storage, the experimental Good Enough File System has made another step toward OpenBSD use. Developer Ori Bernstein reports updated error handling, important fixes carried over from 9front, and userspace tools that can now create a filesystem on OpenBSD. Filesystem developers have concrete new code to test and an open design problem to study. The consistency protocol remains the biggest missing piece, so this belongs on disposable test storage. Crash ordering is very much part of the assignment.

Source 1 Source 2

A Haskell processor learns to talk

Switching to unusual hardware, Ouros runs Haskell programs on a specialized FPGA processor, and its new demonstration adds input and output through a serial connection. Instead of executing conventional instructions, the machine reduces graphs representing function applications. It also supports automatic fine-grained threading and hardware garbage collection. Language implementers and FPGA enthusiasts can explore the simulator or reproduction guide. That's a lovely experiment: change the processor to fit the language, then make the resulting computer say something.

Source 1 Source 2

Explore an eight-bit computer on virtual breadboards

For a more visual hardware experiment, BBRouter's newly shared demonstration puts Ben Eater's eight-bit computer on simulated three-dimensional breadboards. The interface offers schematic views, slowed simulation and single stepping, giving educators a way to connect wires with the behavior they produce. If it loads for you, follow one clock tick through the circuit before reaching for another abstraction.

Source 1 Source 2

A dangling string view haunts a permission check

One last coding puzzle before we play: a new C-plus-plus demonstration shows a permission comparison changing when optimization is enabled. The culprit is undefined behavior: a string view outlives the temporary string it refers to. The author reproduces the surprise with Clang and GCC, under specific conditions. C-plus-plus teachers have a compact lifetime exercise here. Read the example, predict which object owns the characters, and then make ownership explicit.

Source 1 Source 2

Jointter hides words in a dot-and-line graph

And finally, Jointter turns a daily word puzzle into a little graph investigation. Letters are drawn with dots and lines, but most lines start hidden. Guess a word and matching lines stay green; you've got five attempts, with hints spending one. Puzzle designers can explore how partial structure changes the guessing strategy. Today's Monday puzzle uses three letters, and dragging dots only tidies the picture. Go ahead and rearrange the evidence.

Source 1 Source 2

That's Trending Not Peak. Missed something? The links and details are at trending not peak dot com.

  • 01 · Give agent actions a checkpoint

  • 03 · One trainer for several learning stages

  • 05 · A screenshot-heavy agent hits the HTTP ceiling
  • 06 · Test the claim that a framework helps agents
  • 07 · Align image and text models through better examples
  • 08 · Turn a portrait hairstyle into an avatar asset
  • 09 · Make GPU copying respect the array layout
  • 10 · Enlightenment updates the everyday desktop plumbing
  • 11 · Contra takes a new route into the browser
  • 12 · A bootloader that dreams up Linux logs

Full transcript · All story details and sources

Give agent actions a checkpoint

First up, JevAct puts a checkpoint between an agent and selected tool calls. It combines code that checks recorded facts with a decision model that assesses the conversation, then sends rejected actions back for revision. Developers building service agents could explore enforcing business rules without retraining the underlying model. Researchers report consistent gains on telecom and function-calling benchmarks, with mixed airline results. The useful experiment: check a proposed action before it becomes a customer problem.

Source 1 Source 2

Ghostty's terminal engine meets KDE

Next up, Kwi is a new KDE terminal built around Ghostty's reusable terminal engine. KDE supplies the desktop integration, while Qt Quick handles GPU rendering. For Linux developers who spend their day inside terminal applications, that's another way to explore modern terminal features with a familiar desktop interface. Its creator reports substantial benchmark speedups over Konsole, depending on the test. Features are still comparatively limited, so start with your everyday shell and favorite text interface.

Source 1 Source 2

One trainer for several learning stages

Over in training research, a new paper asks whether pretraining, fine-tuning and reinforcement learning need different algorithms. Its unified approach mixes static examples and model-generated learning targets inside one trainer. For teams experimenting with continued training, that opens a different control panel: which data, how much, and when. The small-scale experiments show promising tradeoffs, rather than one universally winning recipe. Try asking whether mixing old material into new training helps your model retain useful abilities.

Source 1 Source 2

A computer phone line as an open board design

Switching to hardware, Koppar has published a USB-C modem board design intended to give a computer LTE data, text messages and voice calls, including call audio over USB. That could interest developers building phone-connected scripts or experimenting with voice agents. The repository includes the original one-page specification and a component review. Working-board trials aren't documented here, so this is a design to inspect before it's a phone line to depend on. Start with the schematic.

Source 1 Source 2

A screenshot-heavy agent hits the HTTP ceiling

Back at the local-model server, a ds4 contributor traced repeated bad-request errors to something delightfully ordinary: too many screenshot bytes. A vision agent kept resending its conversation until it exceeded the server's request limit. An open patch raises that limit and makes it configurable, with reported tests on an M3 Ultra. If your local agent fails after a long visual session, inspect payload size. The patch is pending, and larger requests also mean larger buffered memory allocations.

Source 1 Source 2

Test the claim that a framework helps agents

Speaking of developer choices, Nolan Lawson has built a benchmark for a surprisingly slippery claim: this JavaScript framework is better for coding agents. Agents build the same Pokémon application, then face specification checks and measurements of time, tokens, performance and accessibility. Web teams get a concrete evaluation design to adapt before rewriting an app around that claim. It's one relatively content-heavy application, so the interesting next experiment is your own product's workload, especially if it's much more interactive.

Source 1 Source 2

Before we move from testing applications to training models, thank you to Intelligrit, this episode's sponsor, for supporting Trending Not Peak.

Align image and text models through better examples

Returning to model research, a new JEPA paper explores aligning separately trained image and text encoders. Its key ingredient is training on different observations of the same scene, rather than simply making models bigger. The authors report reaching comparable alignment with forty-two times fewer training samples in their comparison. Multimodal researchers could explore smaller encoders for connecting pictures and descriptions. The theorem depends on specific assumptions, and alignment scores don't establish general language ability. Investigate the training pairs first.

Source 1 Source 2

Turn a portrait hairstyle into an avatar asset

For character creators, VRM Hair Maker packages a very specific pipeline: generate stylized hair from one portrait, preview it on an avatar, and download a VRM file with spring bones included. It builds on HairDeck and bundles the supporting software in a GPU-enabled Docker image. Game developers and avatar tinkerers could try turning a reference hairstyle into a moving asset. The practical test is how it bends and clips on your character. Give that digital haircut a vigorous head shake.

Source 1 Source 2

Make GPU copying respect the array layout

Down in compiler land, Futhark now makes certain GPU copies faster using array-layout information available at runtime. The useful idea is that an array's logical shape and its physical arrangement in memory are separate things. Developers working on numerical tools can explore how that distinction creates optimization opportunities, even for plain copying. The author describes only a small impact on some programs. Still, if you're building an array system, this is a concrete implementation technique to investigate.

Source 1 Source 2

Enlightenment updates the everyday desktop plumbing

On the desktop, Enlightenment's new release adds native PipeWire mixing, a NetworkManager module and integrated clipboard history. For Linux tinkerers exploring another desktop environment, those are practical pieces that make an experiment easier to live in: choose an audio output, manage a VPN, recover copied text. There's also initial NetBSD support. Start with a spare session and test your own networking and audio setup. The interesting possibility is making an alternative desktop fit the tools you already use.

Source 1 Source 2

Contra takes a new route into the browser

Taking that retro turn further, a newly shared Contra port brings the NES game into a browser through WebAssembly. Its creator describes translating assembly to C, then compiling C for the web. The playable interface also offers hosting and joining an online two-player game. For developers curious about software preservation, that's a concrete translation approach to explore alongside the game itself. Multiplayer quality isn't established, so recruit a friend and see how the familiar chaos survives the browser.

Source 1 Source 2

A bootloader that dreams up Linux logs

And finally, BootGPT boots straight into a tiny neural network that invents Linux startup logs. The boot sector itself is five hundred twelve bytes; it loads an additional eleven-and-a-half-kilobyte model and runs without an operating system. For assembly enthusiasts and machine-learning educators, that's a wonderfully compact way to explore inference below the usual software stack. Its eight-character context produces appropriately scrambled output. Try the emulator setup and watch a computer announce hardware that never existed. Extremely confident imaginary peripherals.

Source 1 Source 2

That's Trending Not Peak. Missed something? The links and details are at trending not peak dot com.

Full transcript · All story details and sources

Build defect detection without collecting defects

First up, Roboflow has added anomaly detection, which tackles a wonderfully practical problem: your factory makes too few defective parts to train a defect detector. You train on good examples instead, then flag unusual patches. Its orange demonstration used just two hundred thirty-seven good images. Manufacturers can now explore cloud or local deployment with heatmaps showing suspicious areas. The catch is that different lighting can also look unusual. Validate against your actual production line before trusting the reject bin.

Source 1 Source 2

Tangled makes the forge more separable

Next up, Tangled's new release makes its federated code forge more modular. A separate Svelte interface now uses globally distributed Rust indexers, replacing a single server in Sweden. Developers can self-host selected pieces, such as Git storage or runners, while collaborating through AT Protocol. That's an interesting option for teams wanting more control over their development infrastructure. Migration deserves attention, though: the release also changes its record schemas, and globally distributed reads don't establish the reliability of every supporting service.

Source 1 Source 2

An Apple MLX path from one image to 3D

Over on the Mac, Ivan Fioravanti has started porting Idol's image-to-three-D pipeline to Apple MLX. The underlying model turns one object picture into a Gaussian splat, including guesses about the sides you can't see. That gives graphics developers a local experiment for turning concept art into something they can rotate. The port still uses Apple's MPS backend for some pieces and needs optimization. Don't transfer the original SDK's speed claims to your Mac, or mistake invented geometry for a scan.

Source 1 Source 2

ParticleDB gets a detailed correctness reality check

Before putting agent memory into a new database, here's useful reading: Jepsen's ParticleDB investigation. The database combines SQL, vectors and other workloads, but testing found ninety-six issues, mostly without network faults or multiple clients. Most appeared fixed during testing; committed-write loss and transaction anomalies remained in the last tested build. The vendor says a newer release fixes the rest. Builders get concrete failure cases to evaluate, but that final remediation claim still needs confirmation, and replication wasn't tested.

Source 1 Source 2 Source 3

Coordinate Claude sessions using reported terminal status

Switching to agent plumbing, Rex Claude is a new skill for controlling Claude Code sessions in neighboring terminal panes. Its useful detail is status reporting: a session can say it's working, finished, or waiting on permission, rather than making the coordinator guess from screen text. Developers could use it to compare settings or delegate separate tasks. It requires the Rex terminal and its status integration. Opening more sessions also means coordinating their directories, permissions and edits; the panes don't solve that automatically.

Source 1 Source 2

Simulated interviews improve a psychiatric research agent

Turning to research, a new psychiatric-intake study trains a conversational model with simulated patients, then tests it with psychiatrists role-playing patients. Independent psychiatrists scored the transcripts, and the trained model beat its baseline in roughly seventy-seven percent of matched scenarios. For researchers, that's a concrete method for practicing follow-up questions and stress-testing safety before patient studies. These were structured text encounters with actors, though. Safety failures remained, so the results support further supervised research, not autonomous clinical deployment.

Source 1 Source 2

Kubernetes-style control reaches ESP32 boards

Down at microcontroller scale, kube thirty-two puts a Kubernetes-compatible control plane, an agent and a WebAssembly runtime on ESP thirty-two S-three boards. The appealing experiment is managing tiny devices through familiar orchestration concepts instead of inventing another deployment interface. Embedded developers could explore coordinated sensor or edge workloads with portable WebAssembly programs. Compatibility is the word to inspect carefully: this launch doesn't establish support for every Kubernetes feature, or that a microcontroller can run your existing container images. Tiny cluster, different constraints.

Source 1 Source 2

A quick pause to thank Intelligrit, this episode's sponsor. We've explored what agents can run; coming up, a practical way to learn how to check their work.

Learn the loops around an agent

Back from the break, DeepLearning dot AI has a new Loop Engineering course that builds beyond the basic tool-calling cycle. You add an evaluator, connect external events, then inspect repeated runs to improve the agent's setup. Its example reviews software requirements for ambiguities and missing information, which gives developers a practical project to adapt. This is an intermediate course with code examples, not evidence that an evaluator always catches mistakes. The rubric still has to measure what you actually care about.

Source 1 Source 2

Read once, score several questions

For a more focused model workload, spinf-serve is a newly launched server for bulk classification and decisions. Its design reads a piece of content once and scores multiple questions about it in the same pass, on one GPU. That could suit moderation developers asking several policy questions about each document. The project offers an OpenAI-compatible interface and an Apache license. The supplied evidence doesn't establish throughput or classification accuracy, though; benchmark your question set and check mistakes before replacing a working pipeline.

Source 1 Source 2

Go explains the limits of a TCP vulnerability workaround

On the security side, the Go team has published guidance for a Linux TCP use-after-free vulnerability. Go enables multipath TCP listeners by default starting with version one twenty-four, and the demonstrated remote exploit uses that feature. Operators can disable the default, but explicit socket settings override it, and other attack paths haven't been ruled out. The useful action is checking your deployed kernel's patch status. Treat the application setting as a fragile mitigation; the team's recommended fix is a patched kernel.

Source 1 Source 2

A personal DJ app becomes a browser experiment

Turning to audio, Fraktur is a newly shared DJ mixing app built with the Web Audio API, audio worklets and some Rust. Its creator extracted a full browser version from a personal desktop project, opening a useful playground for musicians and developers curious about interactive audio. The accompanying write-up explains the engineering choices, including bounded track buffers. It's a personal project without a commitment to ongoing support. Try the mixing workflow and your browser's audio behavior before giving it responsibility for an actual dance floor.

Source 1 Source 2

A measured recipe for NixOS on a tiny VPS

Meanwhile, for small-server tinkerers, a new NixOS guide reports getting a system to idle around ninety-six megabytes and complete rebuilds with five hundred twelve megabytes of RAM. The author documents kernel and service changes, along with attempts that didn't help. That's useful material for exploring reproducible systems on constrained virtual machines. These are measurements from one particular template, though. Several changes remove diagnostics or hardware features, so understand each tradeoff rather than copying the whole recipe into a different environment.

Source 1 Source 2

BeOS joins Infinite Mac in the browser

For a little interface archaeology, Infinite Mac now runs multiple BeOS versions in your browser, with streamed disks, preinstalled software and a drive for saving work. Developers and educators can explore a different approach to a multimedia desktop without tracking down vintage hardware. The release also involved upstream emulator fixes for keyboard, graphics and filesystem behavior. That's the caveat and part of the fascination: you're exploring an emulated system whose compatibility required careful repair, not a perfect reconstruction of every original machine.

Source 1 Source 2

Let your agent embarrass itself at Pictionary

And finally, Sketch Stadium lets you connect an agent to a Pictionary-style game. Agents take turns drawing and guessing, which gives developers a playful way to watch pictures and language become a shared task. This is a more entertaining debugging surface than another text-only benchmark. Do not treat the scoreboard as a general intelligence test; the game has not established that. Drawings and guesses are public, so use throwaway agents and prompts. Apparently robots can spend an entire round arguing about a table.

Source 1 Source 2

That's Trending Not Peak. Missed something? The links and details are at trending not peak dot com.

This is Trending Not Peak. Quick note: this podcast uses AI-assisted writing and a synthetic voice. Before we dive in, all the links and details are at trending not peak dot com. Miss something? You can always catch up there.

20 stories. Tap one for its transcript, why we picked it, and source links:

  • 01 · Give agents the metric definitions you already use
  • 02 · An agent backdoor can survive clean training
  • 03 · Overtone fits captions to different screens
  • 04 · PyTorch adds practical Apple Silicon inference paths
  • 05 · A small local model spots sensitive text
  • 06 · Agent coordination needs reading rules
  • 07 · Automatically decline repetitive macOS prompts
  • 08 · Mistral Large 4 arrives with deployment support
  • 09 · Research agents propose more than they can prioritize
  • 10 · Lasm brings Lean toward web runtimes
  • 11 · Teach robot manipulation through human demonstrations
  • 12 · Disease-mention extraction on a CPU
  • 13 · Tax instructions as executable, cited data
  • 14 · Redirect a robot policy while it runs
  • 15 · A dataset for checking compute-growth assumptions
  • 16 · Bivia offers decisions with an abstain option
  • 17 · Exo separates agent mechanisms from editable policy
  • 18 · An AT Protocol privacy surprise for app builders
  • 19 · A multiplayer browser game with flying cats
  • 20 · Doom becomes a neural-network execution engine

Full transcript · All story details and sources

Give agents the metric definitions you already use

First up, a useful fix for agents that confidently calculate the wrong revenue. Google's Knowledge Catalog now generally supports importing business definitions from tools including dbt, Looker and Snowflake. That lets developers ground an assistant in existing metrics instead of rebuilding them. Conflicting definitions retain their origins so people can reconcile them. Google's accuracy gains come from internal benchmarks, though; importing your definitions doesn't establish that your agent follows them correctly.

Source 1 Source 2

An agent backdoor can survive clean training

Next, a security finding for anyone giving models a terminal. Researchers trained small models from scratch with poisoned pretraining data, then used a clean pipeline to turn them into agents. The implanted command-execution backdoor survived. Their four-billion-parameter model triggered roughly ninety-two percent of the time at the tested poison rate. This gives defenders a concrete threat to evaluate, but it doesn't demonstrate that any particular deployed model contains that backdoor.

Source 1 Source 2

Overtone fits captions to different screens

Turning to video, Overtone packages a caption format, a video dot J S plugin, and a command-line tool that turns audio into word-timed captions. The idea is producing captions for different screen shapes from one file. That's handy for developers publishing the same talk across desktop and mobile players. This is a fresh launch, so check transcription, timing and line breaks with your own material before letting it handle the whole publishing pipeline.

Source 1 Source 2

PyTorch adds practical Apple Silicon inference paths

On your development machine, PyTorch two fifteen adds FP8 support and faster mixture-of-experts decoding on Apple Silicon. The project reports about a third more tokens per second for its new decode path. That gives local-model developers something specific to benchmark, alongside new public stream APIs. The release also changes distributed training's default communication backend, so a successful laptop experiment shouldn't stand in for checking your cluster upgrade.

Source 1 Source 2

A small local model spots sensitive text

For privacy tooling, a Mini CPM adapter turns a half-billion-parameter model into a sensitive-text detector, with an integration for Microsoft's Presidio. Developers can explore local detection of names, credentials and medical identifiers before anonymization. The author reports strong token scores, but complete-span results are lower, which matters when one missed character can leave a secret exposed. It also needs a custom loading wrapper; inspect that code and test realistic misses.

Source 1 Source 2

Agent coordination needs reading rules

Meanwhile, agent messaging has an inbox problem. A new study lets messages wait outside an agent's context until its own rules decide what to read. In simulations, that helped large groups coordinate under noisy traffic, where arrival-order reading failed. If you're building collaborating agents, the useful design question becomes which messages deserve attention. These are simulated societies, though, and the best reading rules depend on traffic and each agent's role.

Source 1 Source 2

Automatically decline repetitive macOS prompts

Back on the desktop, dontallow is a tiny Swift utility with a wonderfully literal job: press Don't Allow on macOS local-network permission prompts. The author says it waits without idle CPU use and survives reboots. For developers repeatedly launching apps that shouldn't discover nearby devices, that's a small annoyance removed. Its decision is deliberately automatic, though. Check whether you actually need local-network discovery before delegating that button.

Source 1 Source 2

Mistral Large 4 arrives with deployment support

Moving to open weights, Mistral Large four arrives with Transformers and llama dot cpp support, plus quantized versions. Security teams can explore a model positioned for reproducing vulnerabilities and developing fixes, without depending entirely on an API. Hugging Face describes roughly a trillion total parameters, so open weights don't mean ordinary laptop hardware. Also read the license: it places restrictions on model-as-a-service offerings, and the cybersecurity results aren't a blanket reliability guarantee.

Source 1 Source 2

Research agents propose more than they can prioritize

Speaking of choosing useful work, rTaste tests whether research agents can pick their own best experiments. The study attempted all four hundred fifteen proposals, including the low-ranked ones. Many were judged worthwhile, but rankings weren't shown to beat simply choosing the experiment written first. Researchers could use the released evaluation to test better selection methods. The catch: seven seed papers and model-based auditing leave plenty of room for broader validation.

Source 1 Source 2

Lasm brings Lean toward web runtimes

For a different route to confidence, Lasm brings Lean four to JavaScript and WebAssembly runtimes. Its launch pitches formally verified web applications targeting environments such as Node and the edge. That opens an interesting experiment for developers who want executable logic alongside proofs about that logic. Don't let the phrase verified web app do too much work, though: inspect which properties you've proved and where runtime behavior or external input sits outside them.

Source 1 Source 2

Thanks to Intelligrit for sponsoring this daily update.

Teach robot manipulation through human demonstrations

Into the physical world, Reward AI's OM-one learns manipulation from people wearing a sensor-equipped hand device. The company describes one policy operating across industrial arms and humanoids, with separate controls handling each body's dynamics. That could help robotics teams collect demonstrations without teleoperating every machine. New footage shows package handling and stairs, but a successful sequence isn't a reliability study. Watch repeated trials across different loads, environments and robot bodies.

Source 1 Source 2

Disease-mention extraction on a CPU

Back to smaller models, OpenMed has released a disease-mention extractor with a hundred ninety-four million parameters and an Apache license. It runs locally on a CPU and returns text spans with confidence scores. That could help biomedical developers index documents or build annotation tools without sending text to a hosted model. Finding a disease name doesn't establish a diagnosis, though. Test negation, family history and old conditions before treating extracted mentions as patient facts.

Source 1 Source 2

Tax instructions as executable, cited data

Here's an ambitious paperwork experiment: us-tax-model represents federal income-tax forms and instructions as cited, executable, machine-checkable data. For developers studying rules engines, the useful possibility is tracing a calculation back to its source instead of burying everything in application code. The launch explicitly calls this a proof of concept, and the author says it's AI-generated work. Explore the representation and validation approach; don't mistake that for established filing accuracy.

Source 1 Source 2

Redirect a robot policy while it runs

Returning to robots, LeRobot has introduced an interactive rollout mode that accepts a new instruction while a policy is running. No reset between directions is the appealing part. Robotics developers can use it to explore steering a multitask policy during execution, rather than treating each run as one fixed request. The announcement supports language-conditioned, steerable policies; it doesn't establish that an arbitrary robot can understand an arbitrary new task.

Source 1 Source 2

A dataset for checking compute-growth assumptions

Zooming out, Epoch AI has published an analysis of how much computing capacity new AI-chip sales add each quarter. Its estimate grows about two and a half times annually since twenty twenty-four, slower than the earlier surge. Builders planning infrastructure can explore the underlying dataset and test their assumptions against disclosed sales. This measures estimated capacity additions, not available cloud capacity or prices, and a gap between chip generations may distort the trend.

Source 1 Source 2

Bivia offers decisions with an abstain option

For workflow builders, Articul8's newly launched Bivia returns structured decisions instead of a generated explanation. You supply the state and question; it can choose, score or extract, with an option to abstain when uncertain. That could simplify ticket routing and other repeated judgment calls. The interesting test is calibration: does a confidence score actually predict correctness on your data? The product page's illustrative examples don't answer that, so evaluate before automating consequential decisions.

Source 1 Source 2

Exo separates agent mechanisms from editable policy

Another architecture to explore is Exo, presented in a newly shared research talk. It separates protected agent mechanisms, including history and secrets, from a policy layer that can evolve during execution. Developers experimenting with adaptive agents could borrow that separation when deciding what an agent may rewrite. The presentation announcement reports lower costs on tested tasks, but the supplied material doesn't independently validate those savings or establish that the protection boundary withstands attacks.

Source 1 Source 2

An AT Protocol privacy surprise for app builders

Over in protocol land, a fresh investigation found that an AT Protocol feed reader published subscription URLs, including private feeds, in public records. That's a useful warning for developers building on shared social infrastructure: a familiar interface can conceal a very different storage model. The author describes inspecting more than thirteen hundred subscribed feeds. This is an investigator's report, rather than an independent audit, but it gives builders a concrete data-exposure pattern to check.

Source 1 Source 2

A multiplayer browser game with flying cats

Before our last experiment, a quick browser-game detour: Catcopter puts flying cats into multiplayer battles, complete with paw rotors and catnip. The newly launched game offers several modes and roles, including a mechanic. For web-game developers, it's a playable reference to explore class selection and multiplayer onboarding; for everyone else, it's flying cats. The supplied page doesn't establish networking performance, so try it with friends before declaring your lunch break's tournament infrastructure solved.

Source 1 Source 2

Doom becomes a neural-network execution engine

And finally, Doomformer compiles an integer neural network into a Doom map. Game objects perform arithmetic, while light levels and floor heights store values. The project says it checks every value against NumPy with zero tolerance. For compiler tinkerers and educators, that's a wonderfully strange way to inspect computation through game mechanics. It's an esoteric execution experiment, with no evidence here of practical inference speed. Apparently the demons now have homework.

Source 1 Source 2

That's Trending Not Peak. Missed something? The links and details are at trending not peak dot com.

  • 01 · Odysseys2: did the browser agent actually finish?
  • 02 · Yavashark: an embeddable JavaScript engine
  • 03 · Redox rings: less copying between system services
  • 04 · Popkern: CAD parts as versioned scripts
  • 05 · Managed Deep Agents: hand the browser back to a person
  • 06 · Locals: more agents on one Mac
  • 07 · MiniCPM-OCR on MLX: parse locally, then check
  • 08 · TAO: scheduling around agent tools
  • 09 · OpenCartridge: local game assets in reusable containers
  • 10 · SlideBySide: shared slides without screen sharing
  • 11 · YOLO on AMD: a supported route from training to inference
  • 12 · OmniShowcase: keeping video objects consistent
  • 13 · Async Rust: an explicit state for being done
  • 14 · Nixtamal: keeping NixOS inputs reproducible
  • 15 · Document Parsing Protocol: write down the ambiguous choices
  • 16 · Floe Agent: a development workspace on a tablet
  • 17 · Plushies: squishy Three.js characters for interfaces
  • 18 · Falcon: isolating one speaker in a noisy scene
  • 19 · Qwenputer: a deliberately constructed computer inside a model
  • 20 · Boo Bench: the haunted house for document parsers

Full transcript · All story details and sources

Odysseys2: did the browser agent actually finish?

Our lead today is Odysseys two, a browser-agent benchmark with a very reasonable demand: show your work, including the actual file you produced. Researchers at Carnegie Mellon and Browser Use built a hundred tasks from real user requests. Their strongest tested agent finished fewer than half perfectly. For developers, that's a useful antidote to impressive-looking demos. The tasks and rubrics are available, though automated judging and a changing live web still make comparisons imperfect.

Source 1 Source 2

Yavashark: an embeddable JavaScript engine

Next up, a different kind of JavaScript engine. Yavashark is written in Rust and was announced yesterday. The attraction is embedding JavaScript inside another application, with Rust bindings. The developer reports passing about eighty-two percent of the language test suite. That's progress, with a sizeable asterisk: compatibility is incomplete and speed needs work. Watch small embedded applications first, rather than expecting a browser replacement.

Source 1 Source 2

Redox rings: less copying between system services

Down in operating-system land, Redox has published the results of its ring-buffer project. Applications and system services can exchange requests through shared memory, with less copying along the way. The team also built an asynchronous driver executor and demonstrated storage support. It's plumbing, but the useful kind. The work finished in September; this week's report explains it. Their benchmark gains still need testing against messier, more realistic workloads before we generalize.

Source 1 Source 2

Popkern: CAD parts as versioned scripts

Switching from code to physical parts, Popkern approaches computer-aided design with parts written as scripts and changes organized like database migrations. Its open-source geometry engine runs in a browser or locally, and exports models from the command line. That could suit developers who prefer repeatable scripts to manual edits. The demonstrations include smooth corner blends; test awkward real parts before manufacturing anything expensive.

Source 1 Source 2

Managed Deep Agents: hand the browser back to a person

Next, a practical browser-agent detail. LangChain's Managed Deep Agents can hand you the browser when a site needs a login, then resume after you return control. Browser state can belong to one conversation or follow an authenticated person across conversations. That's useful for testing applications and working with sites without APIs. It's still a beta platform. Shared login state needs care, and the documentation recommends using a direct API when one does the job.

Source 1 Source 2

Locals: more agents on one Mac

Meanwhile, on the Mac, here's Locals. It runs several AI agents on Apple Silicon. Its benchmark reports roughly three times the combined output at eight simultaneous requests, compared with its baseline. Useful if your coding assistants queue for the same model. The practical question is whether that gain holds for your workload. Independent performance checks are the next thing to watch.

Source 1

MiniCPM-OCR on MLX: parse locally, then check

Now, a useful little document pipeline for your Mac. Nativ has brought Mini CPM OCR and its separate checking model to MLX. One model reads the page; the other compares the result with the original. That separation is handy for invoices or archives where confident nonsense is still nonsense. The port is available now, but its small validation set doesn't establish general accuracy. Try your messiest pages before trusting the scores.

Source 1 Source 2

TAO: scheduling around agent tools

Staying with performance, here's TAO. AI agents spend time waiting for tools. This new research scheduler accounts for that waiting when allocating work to graphics processors. The authors report latency reductions of up to twenty-seven percent in their tested setups. The useful idea is coordinating model work with tool readiness. Watch whether those research gains survive the less cooperative workloads of everyday production.

Source 1 Source 2

OpenCartridge: local game assets in reusable containers

For game developers, OpenCartridge packages local asset-generation workflows as cartridges. A canvas interface connects to ComfyUI workers for images, animation and other assets, with the models running on your own hardware. That's an appealing way to keep a working setup together. The documented workers still want a substantial NVIDIA GPU, and the example storage configuration is permissive. Treat it as an early local experiment, and review those defaults before exposing anything to a network.

Source 1 Source 2

SlideBySide: shared slides without screen sharing

For your next technical walkthrough, here's SlideBySide. It lets everyone follow a presentation in their own browser, with shared cursors, drawing, and controls for who can navigate. The appeal is discussing the same diagram without another round of requests to zoom in. Check how your slides look, and read its privacy terms before uploading a confidential deck. Convenience isn't a data policy.

Source 1 Source 2

Thanks to Intelligrit for sponsoring this daily update.

YOLO on AMD: a supported route from training to inference

Switching to computer vision, Ultralytics now officially supports AMD GPUs through ROCm. The practical win is keeping the familiar Python interface for training and inference, with an export path to AMD's inference engine. AMD's guide lists the hardware and workflows it actually tested, which is refreshingly useful. This is Linux support; Windows isn't supported, and WSL hasn't been tested. Check the compatibility list before deciding your spare graphics card has a new career.

Source 1 Source 2

OmniShowcase: keeping video objects consistent

Over in AI video, OmniShowcase tackles objects changing identity as a generated video's camera moves. The researchers reconstruct shape information from several reference pictures, then use it to guide the video. The aim is to keep the same object recognizable from more angles. Product demonstrations are a possible use. For now, it's research with curated benchmarks; watch how it handles ordinary photographs.

Source 1 Source 2 Source 3 Source 4

Async Rust: an explicit state for being done

For the Rust crowd, here's a tiny missing word with surprisingly large consequences: done. Yosh Wuyts argues that async Rust needs a clearer way to represent a future that already returned its value. Polling it again can currently panic or cause other trouble. An explicit finished state could simplify coordination and help embedded use cases. This is a design argument, not a shipped language change. Compatibility is the awkward part.

Source 1 Source 2

Nixtamal: keeping NixOS inputs reproducible

Back to developer tooling, Nixtamal has a walkthrough for building a reproducible NixOS machine. It uses pinned inputs and the system dot nix entry point. The benefit is tying configuration to specific versions, rather than whatever a mutable channel contains. That gives you a more explicit recipe to revisit. This is a specialist workflow, not a new operating system. Watch how it fits your existing configuration.

Source 1 Source 2

Document Parsing Protocol: write down the ambiguous choices

Speaking of documents, what counts as a table when the page is just carefully aligned text? The Document Parsing Protocol tries to make those judgment calls explicit. Its working draft covers tables, forms, marginal notes and other awkward details, with examples and rules for uncertainty. That could make parser evaluations much easier to compare. It's an early proposal, not an established standard. The interesting test is whether different implementations can follow it consistently.

Source 1 Source 2

Floe Agent: a development workspace on a tablet

Now, development on a smaller screen. Floe Agent brings a Linux workspace, terminal, Git, and local web previews to phones and tablets. It's built around the iPad; Android remains in alpha. The appeal is a familiar development workflow without carrying a laptop. But local workspace doesn't automatically mean local AI: cloud models still send requests away. Check which backend you're using.

Source 1

Plushies: squishy Three.js characters for interfaces

And a small treat for people building interfaces: Plushies turns simple shapes into squishy three-dimensional characters using Three dot J S. There's a browser editor, reusable code, and animated cursors that can show what an assistant is doing. The demo is very cute; it is also a demo, not evidence that your agent became more capable. For a real application, the interesting test is whether the character communicates useful status without getting in the way.

Source 1 Source 2

Falcon: isolating one speaker in a noisy scene

Turning to audio, Falcon combines sound with video of a speaker's mouth to separate that voice from a noisy scene. Published last week, the research reports lower compute costs than its comparison model, with simulated and recorded evaluations. Meeting transcription is a plausible application. The catch is needing useful video of the target speaker. Watch what happens when faces are obscured or the camera moves.

Source 1 Source 2 Source 3 Source 4

Qwenputer: a deliberately constructed computer inside a model

Now for something a little stranger. Qwenputer constructs a deterministic processor inside a language model by compiling its operations into model weights. Last week's write-up describes engineered computation, not a model spontaneously learning to become a computer. It's an intriguing bridge between compilers and neural networks, worth watching for independent reproductions and clearer practical applications. Your laptop probably needn't feel threatened yet.

Source 1 Source 2

Boo Bench: the haunted house for document parsers

And finally, a haunted house for document parsers. LlamaIndex's Boo Bench has a hundred and seventy-nine pages designed to make models repeat themselves. In one example, a page with a few hundred letter Xs produced more than twenty-three thousand. Apparently the ghost is a stuck keyboard. The dataset includes real pages and deliberately tricky ones. It's a useful stress test, not a complete accuracy ranking. Happy Halloween to everyone debugging a PDF.

Source 1 Source 2

That's Trending Not Peak. Missed something? The links and details are at trending not peak dot com.
